title: Requests per second

public.prompt: A service handles 2 billion requests per day, spread evenly. What is its average requests per second?

explanation: A day has 86,400 seconds (round it to ~10^5 when estimating). 2×10^9 / 8.64×10^4 ≈ 23,000 QPS. Senior habit: say the average, then immediately size for peak (often 2–5× the average).

title: A year of short posts

public.prompt: A social app stores 500 million text posts per day at ~300 bytes each (text plus metadata, no media). How many bytes for one year, before replication and indexes?

explanation: 5×10^8 posts × 300 B = 1.5×10^11 B/day ≈ 150 GB/day. × 365 ≈ 5.5×10^13 B ≈ 55 TB/year. Real systems multiply by the replication factor (×3) and add indexes, so plan for roughly 200 TB.

title: Session cache size

public.prompt: You cache a 1 KB session object for each of 100 million users. Ignoring overhead, how much memory is that?

explanation: 10^8 × 10^3 B = 10^11 B = 100 GB. That's more than one comfortable cache node, so it needs sharding. Real caches also add per-key overhead (often tens of bytes), which matters with small values.

title: Integers in a gibibyte

public.prompt: How many 64-bit integers fit in 1 GiB of memory (a plain array)?

explanation: 1 GiB = 2^30 bytes and each long is 8 = 2^3 bytes, so 2^27 ≈ 1.34×10^8. Boxed Long objects in a Java collection cost several times more per element (object header plus reference), so 'fits in memory' depends heavily on representation.

title: Main-memory reads per second

public.prompt: Using the classic latency rule of thumb that a main-memory reference costs ~100 ns, how many dependent (one-after-another, cache-missing) memory references can one core make per second?

explanation: 1 s / 100 ns = 10^7. This is why pointer-chasing structures (linked lists, trees of objects) are slow compared with scanning arrays, where caches and prefetching hide the latency.

title: Moving 10 TB

public.prompt: How many seconds does it take to transfer 10 TB over a 1 Gbps link running at full utilisation?

explanation: 10 TB = 8×10^13 bits. At 10^9 bits/s that's 8×10^4 s ≈ 22 hours. Bytes vs bits is the classic trap (×8). For large migrations, shipping physical drives or using a cloud transfer appliance can beat the network.

title: Video egress

public.prompt: 10 million daily active users each watch 30 minutes of 3 Mbps video per day. What is the average egress bandwidth in bits per second?

explanation: Per user: 1,800 s × 3×10^6 b/s = 5.4×10^9 bits/day. × 10^7 users = 5.4×10^16 bits/day. ÷ 86,400 ≈ 6.25×10^11 b/s ≈ 625 Gbps on average. Peak is higher, which is why video platforms rely on CDNs.

title: PostgreSQL heap pages

public.prompt: A PostgreSQL table has 50 million rows of ~200 bytes of data each. Each row also carries a ~24-byte tuple header and a 4-byte line pointer. Pages are 8 KB. Ignoring fill factor and TOAST, roughly how many heap pages does it need?

explanation: ≈228 bytes per row, so about 8,192 / 228 ≈ 35 rows per page. 5×10^7 / 35 ≈ 1.4×10^6 pages ≈ 11 GB. Per-row overhead is significant for narrow rows, which is one reason column choice and data types matter at scale.

title: UUID collisions

public.prompt: A random UUIDv4 has 122 random bits. Roughly how many UUIDs must you generate before there is a ~50% chance of at least one collision?

explanation: Birthday bound: about 1.18 × sqrt(N) for N = 2^122 possible values, so 1.18 × 2^61 ≈ 2.7×10^18. In practice, collisions come from bad randomness (e.g. cloned VM seeds), not from the maths.

title: Tokens in a megabyte

public.prompt: A common rule of thumb for English text and typical LLM tokenizers is about 4 characters per token. Roughly how many tokens is 1 MB of plain English text?

explanation: 10^6 characters / 4 ≈ 2.5×10^5 tokens. Useful for sizing context windows, chunking for RAG and estimating API cost. Code and non-English text usually take more tokens per character, so measure with the real tokenizer before committing.

title: Embedding memory

public.prompt: You store 10 million embeddings of 1,536 dimensions as float32 for vector search. How much memory do the raw vectors take (no index overhead)?

explanation: 10^7 × 1,536 × 4 B ≈ 6.1×10^10 B ≈ 61 GB before any HNSW graph overhead. That drives choices such as quantisation (int8 is 4× smaller), fewer dimensions, or disk-based indexes.

title: Blocking worker throughput

public.prompt: A worker processes one request at a time, and each request spends 50 ms blocked on a database call (CPU time is negligible). How many requests per second can one worker handle?

explanation: 1 s / 50 ms = 20. To serve 2,000 req/s you'd need ~100 concurrent workers or threads, or non-blocking I/O or virtual threads. Little's Law gives the same answer: concurrency = throughput × latency.
